abstract: Aquilaria sinensis (Agarwood) is a precious Chinese medicine commonly used in clinical practice. Previous researches about agarwood mainly focused on chemical composition, pharmacological activities and artificial induction. The molecular processes responsible for agarwood formation remain largely unknown. This study performs an integrated proteomic and metabolomic analysis of agarwood after treatment with fire (F) or fire plus different concentrations of salt (FSH, FSM, FSL) for 4 and 12 months. A total of 1611 differential metabolites and 9148 differentially expressed proteins were detected in 30 samples of agarwood. The fire plus 0.4 mol/L NaCl (FSM) treatment induced more differential metabolites compared to fire plus 0.04 mol/L NaCl (FSL) and fire plus 4 mol/L NaCl (FSH) at both 4 and 12 month. The primary differential categories included organic acids, sesquiterpenoids, phenolic acids, flavonoids, and chromones. KEGG analysis indicated significant enrichment of secondary metabolite biosynthesis, ABC transporters, and flavonoid biosynthesis pathways across all comparison groups. Additionally, all six comparison groups revealed different levels of 2-(2-phenylethyl) chromones (PECs), the distinctive constituents of agarwood. Nevertheless, the fire plus 0.04 mol/L NaCl (FSL) treatment produced the most differentially expressed proteins compared to fire plus 0.4 mol/L NaCl (FSM) and fire plus 4 mol/L NaCl (FSH). Sesquiterpene synthases were significantly upregulated in the F1(fire drill in the 4th month)_vs_FSH1(fire drill + 4 mol/L NaCl in the 4th month) and F1_vs_FSL1(fire drill + 0.04 mol/L NaCl in the 4th month) group, but downregulated in the F3(fire drill in the 12th month)_vs_FSH3(fire drill + 4 mol/L NaCl in the 12th month) group. Besides, the varying expression levels of these candidate proteins (HMGS, PMK and TPS) involved in the sesquiterpene biosynthesis pathway across the different stress treatments provide valuable insights into their roles in biological mechanism of agarwood formation. Proteomics and metabolomics analyses of agarwood provide essential insights into its formation mechanisms and support quality enhancement initiatives. Supplementary Information The online version contains supplementary material available at 10.1186/s12870-025-07357-1.
methods:
Materials and methods
Plant materials and treatments
Agarwood samples were derived from 10-year-old
Aquilaria sinensis
trees cultivated in Xiashuang Village, Pingding Town, Huazhou City, Guangdong Province, China (110°27′7″N, 22°45′5″E). We have obtained permission to collect “
Aquilaria sinensis”.
All samples were divided into five groups: CK (blank control, untreated white agarwood), F (fire drill), FSH (fire drill + high salt, an aqueous solution of 4 mol/L NaCl), FSM (medium salt, 0.4 mol/L NaCl), FSL (low salt, 0.04 mol/L NaCl). Each group included 15 plants. For the fire drill treatment, a hole was drilled every 30 cm from the base of the tree (diameter 2 cm) to the height of the tree (3 ~ 4 m), and the upper and lower holes were arranged in a straight line. Fire drill + salt was injected 50 ~ 80 mL NaCl solution of different concentrations into each hole within 1 h after drilling the hole. A total of nine agarwood trees were randomly cut down for each treatment. After removing the white wood, the samples of agarwood tablets were obtained and brought back to the laboratory for natural air drying and crushing. During each sampling, the outer, middle and inner parts of all samples are selected for each treatment to make mixed samples. Next time, the target tree will not be repeated in the same position to avoid damaging affect the experimental results. When sampling and determination, the wood chips around the discolored part of the fire hole were taken with a knife. The wood chips were sampled by layers according to the white wood layer, the transition layer (the fragrant layer) and the discolored layer (the rotten wood layer). Wood samples were stored in liquid nitrogen within an ultra-low temperature freezer at −80 °C. Samples were collected in the 4th month (CK1, F1, FSH1, FSM1, FSL1) and the 12th month (CK3, F3, FSL3, FSM3, FSH3) post-treatment. The 4th and 12th month sampling is for Living samples, and the 13th month sampling is for tree felling and sampling of the discolored layer which develops into a fragrant layer. Agarwood tablets were collected after 13 months of treatment. The specific purpose of 13-month sampling is to test the quality (oil content, composition) of agarwood. In addition, fresh wood samples were fixed in FAA fixative for over 24 h and then sectioned with a razor blade. Sections were stained with 0.5% auramine O solution for 30 min, followed by two washes with distilled water. The stained sections were mounted on slides with distilled water and examined under a fluorescence microscope using 388 nm UV light for observation and photography. The specific method flowchart is shown in the following figure.
Metabolome analysis
A comprehensive metabolomics approach was employed to analyze metabolites in both control and treatment groups. Metabolite extraction, detection, identification, and quantification were carried out in the Wuhan MetWare Biotechnology Co., Ltd. The ESI source was configured with a source temperature of 500 ℃ and an ion spray voltage of 5500 V for positive ion mode and − 4500 V for negative ion mode. The ion source gases I and II were set to 50 psi and 60 psi, respectively, with the curtain gas at 25 psi. Collision activation dissociation was set to a high level. The QQQ scanning was performed as an MRM experiment with medium-level nitrogen collision gas. Optimize the clustering potential (DP) and collision energy (CE) for an individual MRM transition. For each period, monitor a specific set of MRM transformations corresponding to the eluted metabolites.
Proteomics analysis
Proteins were isolated from the samples using the acetone precipitation technique. Combine the protein solution with four times its volume of frozen acetone and allow it to precipitate at −20 °C overnight. Centrifuge the mixture at 4 °C to collect the precipitate, which should then be washed with cold acetone and dissolved in 8 M urea. Finally, the protein concentration was determined with a BCA kit according to the instructions of the manufacturer. Liquid chromatography (LC) was conducted using a nanoElute UHPLC system from Bruker Daktronics, Germany.
Integrated proteomics and metabolomics analysis
The functions and pathways of the differentially expressed proteins and metabolites were determined using the KEGG mapper reconstruction pathway analysis tool (
https://www.kegg.jp/blastkoala/
accessed on 15 December 2021) and the M. esculenta (cassava) proteome dataset, which was annotated based on literature and PubChem data (
https://pubchem.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/
accessed on 15 December 2021). A protein–protein interaction network was constructed using STRING, version 11.5, and STITCH, version 5.0 (
http://stitch.embl.de/
accessed on 20 December 2021) and used for mapping the interactions between the proteins and metabolites.
Quantitative real‑time PCR (qRT‑PCR) validation
qRT-PCR was used to measure the expression levels of eight genes involved in the sesquiterpene biosynthesis pathway, which were performed using the SYBR Green QPCR Mix (DF Biotech., Chengdu, China). Total RNA was isolated from frozen flesh tissue using the TRUEscript RT MasterMix (DF Biotech., Chengdu, China) according to manufacturer’s instructions. An aliquot (2 mg) of total RNA was used for first-strand cDNA synthesis with the TransScript First-Strand cDNA Synthesis kit (AiDLAB Biotech, Beijing, P.R. China). The qRT-PCR protocol began with an initial denaturation at 95 °C for 2 min, followed by 40 cycles consisting of 95 °C for 5 s, and 60 °C for 30 s. All data were obtained from three biological repetitions and three technical replicates with
GAPDH
as an internal control. The genes expression levels of the genes were determined calculated using the 2
−ΔΔCt
method.
Statistical analysis
In two-group analysis, differential metabolites were identified using VIP scores greater than 1 and an absolute Log
2
FC of at least 1.0. VIP values along with score and permutation plots, were derived from the OPLS-DA results using the MetaboAnalystR package. The data underwent log2 transformation and mean centering prior to OPLS-DA. A permutation test with 200 iterations was conducted to prevent overfitting. DIA raw MS data were processed using DIA-NN (v1.8.1) with a spectral library approach. Specified the Identification result of DDA as a spectral library, the option of MBR was employed to create a spectral library from DIA data and then re-analyse using this library. The false discovery rate (FDR) for search results was adjusted to below 1% at both the protein and precursor ion levels, and the remaining identifications were utilized for subsequent quantification analysis.

body:
Introduction
Aquilaria sinensis
is a key resin-producing plant known for generating agarwood, a recognized traditional Chinese medicine resource [
1
]. Agarwood, known as “Chenxiang” in Chinese, is a valuable aromatic resin produced by
Aquilaria
trees in response to mechanical damage, insect attacks, or microbial invasion [
2
]. Agarwood, known for its diverse secondary metabolites, is extensively utilized as a valuable spice, traditional medicine, aromatic food additive, and incense in religious rituals across China, Japan, India, and other Southeast Asian nations [
3
,
4
]. Research has identified over 300 chemical compounds in agarwood, such as sesquiterpenes, 2-(2-phenylethyl) chromones, and flavonoids [
5
]. Wang Anjun et al. [
6
] conducted metabolic analysis and transcriptome sequencing of six distinct tissues (root, stem, leaf, seed, husk, and callus) of
A. sinensis
to investigate the variations in metabolite distribution characteristics and transcriptome data across different tissues. A previous study [
7
] found that 6-methoxy-2-(2-phenylethyl)chromone and 6,7-dimethoxy-2-(2-phenylethyl)chromone were significant markers detected by both GC-MS and UPLC-Q-TOF-MS, which may be essential substances responsible for differences in the agarwood-forming capacities of the cut sections. Sesquiterpenes and 2-(2-phenylethyl) chromones, the main constituents of agarwood extracts, exhibit diverse pharmacological activities, including antibacterial, antifungal, and anti-inflammatory effects. Contemporary pharmacological studies indicate that agarwood positively influences the nervous system and is clinically employed to treat anxiety and depression, demonstrating low toxicity and high safety [
8
,
9
]. Chromones, sesquiterpenoids, flavonoids, benzophenones and phorbol esters were the major anti-inflammatory compounds isolated from
Aquilaria species
[
10
]. Consequently, there is significant global demand for agarwood. Recently, increasing attention has been directed towards methods for inducing agarwood formation. The quality and yield of agarwood produced through artificial methods such as the burn-chisel-drill technique [
11
], formic acid application [
12
], and fungal infestation [
2
], remain unsatisfactory. High-quality agarwood, often referred to as the wood of gods, develops very slowly, sometimes taking several hundred years, while global market demand continues to rise. Gaining molecular insights into agarwood formation can enhance its quality and yield.
Agarwood formation primarily involves significant resin deposition in the xylem rays, axial thin-walled cells, xylem phloem, vessels, and wood fibers [
13
,
14
]. The deposition of resin darkens the color of wood, producing a special odor and enhancing its biological activity [
15
,
16
]. Under stress, trees activate parenchyma cells to trigger defense mechanisms and engage in physiological metabolic activities, leading to the induction of phenylalanine ammonia lyase (PAL) and the accumulation of secondary metabolite [
17
]. Stress in trees leads to increased membrane lipid peroxidation, accumulation of malondialdehyde (MDA), and disruption of cellular metabolism. Simultaneously, the activities of catalase (CAT) and superoxide dismutase (SOD) significantly increase, effectively removing excess reactive oxygen species (ROS), protecting membrane structures, and promoting sustainable tree survival. In addition, stored substances undergo translocation and transformation in thin-walled cells, initiating secondary metabolism and ultimately forming agarwood.
In recent years, the analysis of metabolites in agarwood has received increasing attention in its quality control, and studies have shown a correlation between the quality of agarwood and its metabolites [
18
,
19
]. Metabolomics seeks to thoroughly analyze all metabolites in biological samples, offering significant potential for understanding plant metabolic processes. Advancements in instrumentation and analysis have significantly enhanced the application and sensitivity of metabolomics in recent years. Advancements in this technology have enabled more frequent and precise large-scale metabolomic studies of rarely studied plant species. For millennia, humans have utilized plants’ secondary metabolites for nutrition, materials, and medicine. Numerous traditional Chinese medicine formulations utilize plant secondary metabolites for disease treatment. Limited research has documented the proteomic profiles of agarwood subjected to various treatments. To date, no comprehensive analysis combining proteomics and metabolomics in agarwood has been reported. A multi-omics study using the same experimental setup is essential for an integrated understanding of dehydration-induced physiological phenomena and the mechanisms underlying desiccation tolerance.
In the present study, through the joint analysis of proteome and metabolome within the fragrance layer of agarwood under different stress treatments, the relationship between differential metabolites and proteins was explored. Simultaneously, functional analysis and metabolic pathway enrichment were integrated to examine the biological molecular functions and regulatory mechanisms. A thorough understanding of biological change trends and directions was achieved, leading to the proposal of a molecular biology change mechanism model. Key proteins and metabolites, including sesquiterpenes and chromones, were selected to further investigate high-quality agarwood. This provides a theoretical foundation for human intervention and regulation of the aroma process, which is crucial for addressing the scarcity of agarwood resources.

Agarwood formation
A few months later after injecting agarwood inducer, resin-like wood formed around the wound parts. The black resinous wood of the trees treated by fire, fire and salt with different concentration are shown in Fig.
1
. Plants without any treatment were used as control group (CK). We have set two sampling times, four months (sample numbers: CK1, F1, FSH1, FSM1, FSL1) (Fig.
1
A) and 12 months (sample numbers: CK3, F3, FSL3, FSM3, FSH3) (Fig.
1
B). And we collected the agarwood fragrance slices on the 13th month. Interestingly, resin wood was found on the tree trunks. However, The CK group remained as white wood without forming any resin. Agarwood inducers are crucial for the development of resinous wood.

Widely targeted metabolome analyses among different treatments of Agarwood
Metabolomic analysis of the aroma layer of agarwood under stress treatment at different stages were performed. Post-treatment, agarwood layers underwent metabolic profiling using liquid chromatography-mass spectrometry (LC-MS). Supplementary Fig. 1 presents the superimposed ion flow diagrams for all samples, continuously depicted in mass spectrometry at each time point, alongside the multimodal diagrams of MRM metabolite detection. Furthermore, the heatmap analysis was carried out for all samples (Fig.
3
A), some metabolites of agarwood were up-regulated when under fire stress, but down-regulated under salt stress, suggesting that agarwood under different stress treatment might undergo significantly different metabolic processes. Principal component analysis (PCA) was employed to compare the 1611 metabolites across various stress treatments of agarwood. Metabolites from various agarwood stress treatments were distinctly separated in score plots, with the first principal component (PC1) plotted against the second (PC2). PC1 and PC2 accounted for 41.07% and 23.72% of the total variation, respectively (Fig.
3
B). Furthermore, a total of 1611 metabolites were divided into 12 classes, including 15.89% flavonoids, 11.79% amino acids and derivatives, 10.43% terpenoids, 9.75% phenolic acid, 8.07% alkaloids, 7.76% Lipids, 5.96% Lignans and coumarins, 3.544% nucleotides and derivatives and 19.37% others (Fig.
3
C).

Likewise, there were 244 (129 upregulated and 115 downregulated) detected in F3_vs_FSH3, and 262 differential metabolites (122 upregulated and 140 downregulated) in the F3_vs_FSM3 group, 202 differential metabolites (91 upregulated and 111 downregulated) detected in the F3_vs_FSL3 group, respectively, and 49 metabolites were mutual in the three comparison groups. There were 582 (276 upregulated and 306 downregulated) detected in FSH1_vs_FSH3, and 435 differential metabolites (300 upregulated and 135 downregulated) in the FSM1_vs_FSM3 group, 647 differential metabolites (318 upregulated and 329 downregulated) detected in the FSL1_vs_FSL3 group, respectively.

And three phenolic acids Eugenyl benzoate, 2-Hydroxycinnamic acid* and 4-Allyl-2,6-dimethoxyphenol were upregulated in the F3_vs_FSM3 group. In the F3_vs_FSM3 group, two chromones were identified: 4’-Methoxyflavone, which was downregulated, and 2-(2-Phenylethyl)chromone, which was upregulated. In the F3_vs_FSL3 group, two sesquiterpenoids, 12-hydroxy-4(5),11(13)-eudesmadien-15-al and Confertifoline, were identified as upregulated. In F3_vs_FSL3 group, the flavonoids Ayanin (3’,5-Dihydroxy-3,4’,7-Trimethoxyflavone) and Aromadendrin-7-O-glucoside were downregulated. The top 10 differential metabolites in FSH1_vs_FSH3, FSM1_vs_FSM3 and FSL1_vs_FSL3 were shown in Table
3
. The top twenty compounds with the most significant differences (VIP > 1) across all comparisons were identified (Fig.
6
). The primary differential categories included organic acids, sesquiterpenoids, phenolic acids, flavonoids, and chromones.

Integrated proteomics and metabolomics analysis
As shown in Supplementary Fig. 2, the integrated proteomics and metabolomics analysis identified that DEPs and DAMs in agarwood were enriched in 11 KEGG pathways, including Biosynthesis of amino acids, Biosynthesis of cofactors, Pyruvate metabolism, Phenylpropanoid biosynthesis, and Cysteine and methionine metabolism. To better understand the relationship between metabolomics and proteomics, we also used Cytoscape to analyze the KEGG pathways network of DAMs and DEPs.
Discussion
Agarwood, a fragrant wood, is extensively utilized in medicine and incense, which is known as “gold in medicine” and “king of incense” [
20
]. Under normal conditions, healthy plants cannot produce agarwood [
21
]. The process of agarwood forms remains uncertain. Investigating defense systems, particularly early damage-responsive proteins and metabolites, is crucial for comprehending agarwood formation [
22
]. According to previous studies, agarwood is not produced in healthy trees, and its formation is related to tissue damage and invasion by biotic or abiotic agents. Mechanical injury can induce early response of wound responsive proteins and metabolites three hours after injury [
2
,
23
]. This study integrates metabolomics and proteomics analyses of aroma layer tissues subjected to varying NaCl gradients under fire drill conditions, laying the groundwork for understanding the dual-factor mixed induction aroma mechanism of agarwood. A total of 1611 differential metabolites and 9148 differentially expressed proteins were detected in 30 samples of agarwood. After comparison among different treatments, we concluded that the fire plus 0.4mol/L NaCl(FSM) induced more differential metabolites compared to fire plus 0.04 mol/L NaCl (FSL) and fire plus 4 mol/L NaCl (FSH) at the 4th month. And the fire plus 0.04 mol/L NaCl induced the most differentially expressed proteins compared to fire plus 0.4 mol/L NaCl (FSM) and fire plus 4 mol/L NaCl (FSH) at the 4th month.
Agarwood is extensively utilized in traditional Chinese medicine for enhancing qi circulation, alleviating pain, warming the middle, nourishing qi, inducing vomiting, regulating breathing, and treating asthma [
24
]. It serves as a sedative to alleviate excitement. In traditional Chinese medicine, agarwood is commonly utilized as a qi-regulating agent for the fumigation treatment of gastrointestinal disorders, cough, rheumatism, and high fever. 2-(2-phenylethyl)chromones (PECs), key components of agarwood, exhibit diverse biological activities and serve as quality indicators in the Chinese Pharmacopoeia [
25
,
26
]. Therefore, the mechanisms for the induction of PECs are important for studies on agarwood formation. According to reports, 54 types of 2- (2-phenylethyl) pigments have been isolated from various agarwood plants [
21
,
27
]. Yan [
28
] demonstrated that varying induction techniques lead to differing levels of 2-(2-phenylethyl)chromones in agarwood. Agarwood induction methods yield different PEC content levels. However, its biosynthetic mechanism is currently unclear. The study identified two PECs, 6,8-dihydroxy-2-(2-phenylethyl)chromone and 7-hydroxy-2-(2-phenylethyl)chromone, which were upregulated in FSH1 compared to F1. In the F1_vs_FSM1 group, 6,7-Dimethoxy-2-(2-phenylethyl) chromone was upregulated, while 6,8-Dihydroxy-2-(2-phenylethyl) chromone, 5-Hydroxy-6-methoxy-2-(2-phenylethyl)chromone, 7-hydroxy-2-(2-phenylethyl) chromone, 7-Methoxy-2-(2-phenylethyl)chromone, and 6-Methoxy-2-(2-phenylethyl)chromone were downregulated. The compound 6,8-dihydroxy-2-(2-phenylethyl)chromone was upregulated in the F1_vs_FSL1 comparison. The F3_vs_FSH3 group showed increased levels of 7-hydroxy-2-(2-phenylethyl)chromone, 2-(2-Phenylethyl)chromone, and 6,8-Dihydroxy-2-(2-phenylethyl)chromone. The F3_vs_FSM3 group showed upregulation of 2-(2-Phenylethyl)chromone, 7-hydroxy-2-(2-phenylethyl)chromone, and 6,7-Dimethoxy-2-(2-phenylethyl)chromone. These results indicated that fire and fire plus salt stress treatments can produce agarwood with varying PEC contents.
Chromones are one of the major classes of naturally occurring compounds and possess significant biological activities such as anti-tumor, antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, and antibacterial properties [
29
]. Chemically, chromones are heterocyclic compounds with a benzopyranone ring.
Aquilaria
are among the few plant species that can produce 2-(2-phenylethyl)chromone, which is a characteristic component of agarwood and is also an indicator component for evaluating the quality of agarwood in the Chinese Pharmacopoeia [
24
]. The biosynthetic mechanism of this compound remains unclear. In the present study, we found that four chromones including 7-Methoxy-2-(2-Phenylethyl)Chromone, 6-hydroxy-7-methoxy-2-(4-methoxyphenethyl)−4 H-chromen-4-one, 6-Methoxy-2-(4-methoxyphenethyl)chromone and 6,8-Dihydroxy-2-(2-phenylethyl)chromone were highly accumulated in the FSM1 group compared with F1 group. Furthermore, 2-(2-hydroxy-2-(4-hydroxyphenyl)ethyl)−6,7-dimethoxy-4 H-chromen-4-one, 7-hydroxy-6-methoxy-2-[2-(3’-hydroxy-4’-methoxyphenyl)ethyl]chromone, 6-hydroxy-2-(3-hydroxy-4-methoxyphenethyl)−7-methoxy-4 H-chromen-4-one and 2-(2-hydroxy-2-(4-hydroxyphenyl)ethyl)−6,7-dimethoxy-4 H-chromen-4-one were highly accumulated in the FSL1 group compared with F1 group. The results further confirmed that the sensitivity of agarwood responding to fire and fire plus salt stress treatments is different so that could invoke different biological processes in response to wounding stress.
Flavonoids present in
Aquilaria
spp. exceed the quantity of other compound classes [
15
]. A total of thirty-six compounds have been isolated from
Aquilaria
plants. Thirty-two compounds have been isolated from
A. sinensis
, with some also reported in
A. crassna
and
A. agallocha
.
Apigenin
(AF1) is exclusively derived from
A. agallocha
. While
Aquilaria
plants contain numerous flavonoids, agarwood has been reported to contain only one flavonoid, 5-hydroxy-40,7-dimethoxyflavone (AF5). The pathways ‘Biosynthesis of secondary metabolites’ and ‘Flavonoid biosynthesis’ were significantly enriched across all comparison groups. Flavonoid biosynthetic pathways are extensively researched across various plant species [
30
–
32
]. In the F1_vs_FSH1 group, flavonoids such as Epicatechin are upregulated, whereas 5,7,3’,4’-Tetrahydroxy-6,8-dimethoxyflavone is downregulated. In the F1_vs_FSM1 group, the flavonoid category features the upregulation of Tupichinol E and Quercetin-3-O-glucoside (Isoquercitrin)*. Upregulated 5,7,3’,4’-Tetrahydroxy-6,8-dimethoxyflavone was identified in F1_vs_FSL. In the F3_vs_FSH3 group, upregulated Epicatechin-epiafzelechin was identified. Downregulated 4’-Methoxyflavone was found in F3_vs_FSM3 group. In the F3_vs_FSL3 group, both Ayanin (3’,5-Dihydroxy-3,4’,7-Trimethoxyflavone) and Aromadendrin-7-O-glucoside exhibited downregulation. These results may be the reason for the medicinal differences among different stress treatments in agarwood.
Sesquiterpenoids are a primary and distinctive chemical component of agarwood, integral to its medicinal properties. In agarwood, sesquiterpene is a key component that develops in the stems, branches, or roots of
A. sinensis
upon injury [
33
]. Up to now, domestic and foreign scholars have isolated and identified more than 20 sesquiterpenoid components from agarwood, which comes from the source of white wood [
15
,
34
]. Researchers have extensively studied the significance of sesquiterpenes in agarwood [
35
]. Sesquiterpenoids are mainly synthesized through a series of reactions of the MVA pathway [
36
], where HMGS and HMGR have been recognized as important enzymes. Further, PMK is an important ATP-dependent enzyme that regulates the construction of the sesquiterpene backbone [
37
]. Additionally, the expression of TPS genes is important for the synthesis of terpenes. In this study, the HMGS proteins (MBA0621632.1,
KAH7276395.1
and MCD7452097.1) were highly expressed in FSM1, FSH1 and FSL1 groups as compared to CK1 and F1. The expression levels of TPS including
ALR84835.1
,
KAH0451797.1
,
CDP19753.1
,
AAV68713.1
and
KAI5413368.1
were significantly increased in F1, FSM1 and FSH1 groups as compared to CK1 and FSL1. These results indicate an increased sesquiterpene synthesis in agarwood with fire drill + salt treatments. The varying expression levels of these candidate proteins (HMGS, PMK and TPS) across the different stress treatments provide valuable insights into their roles in biological mechanism of agarwood formation.
All identified guaiane sesquiterpenes were unsaturated, with some featuring oxygenation. Sesquiterpenes possess distinct odors that contribute to the aroma of agarwood. The study found an upregulation of 1β-hydroxy-4(15),5E,10(14)-germacratriene in FSH1 relative to F1. The compound 12-hydroxy-4(5),11(13)-eudesmadien-15-al was found to be downregulated in the F1_vs_FSM1 group. Similarly, the sesquiterpenoids Neopetasane, 7β-H-9(10)-ene-11,12-epoxy-8-oxoeremophilane, and 12-hydroxy-4(5),11(13)-eudesmadien-15-al showed increased expression in FSH3 relative to F3. Baimuxiangic acid and Ilicic acid were upregulated in F3_vs_FSM3 group. The F1_vs_FSL1 group exhibited upregulation of 12-hydroxy-4(5),11(13)-eudesmadien-15-al and Confertifoline. Furthermore, sesquiterpene synthase was upregulated in the F1_vs_FSH1, F1_vs_FSL1 and downregulated in the F3_vs_FSH3. Sesquiterpene synthase is the most important catalytic enzyme for the biosynthesis of sesquiterpene compounds of agarwood [
38
]. Therefore, we speculated that sesquiterpene synthase play crucial role in the mechanism of agarwood formation. These results indicated that fire and fire plus salt stress treatments can produce agarwood with varying sesquiterpenoids. We speculate that the fire plus salt stress treatment could produce agarwood with better quality.
Conclusions
Analysis of proteomics and metabolomics in agarwood under various stress treatments showed alterations in protein abundance and metabolite regulation. A total of 1611 metabolites were detected in 30 samples of agarwood. The primary differential categories included organic acids, sesquiterpenoids, phenolic acids, flavonoids, and chromones. The fire plus 0.4 mol/L NaCl(FSM) induced the most differential metabolites compared to fire plus 0.04 mol/L NaCl (FSL) and fire plus 4 mol/L NaCl (FSH) at the 4th month. The fire plus 0.04 mol/L NaCl induced the most differentially expressed proteins at the 4th month. Besides, the varying expression levels of these candidate proteins (HMGS, PMK and TPS) across the different stress treatments provide valuable insights into their roles in biological mechanism of agarwood formation. These results indicated that fire and fire plus salt stress treatments can produce agarwood with varying PEC and sesquiterpenoids contents. We speculate that the fire plus salt stress treatment could produce agarwood with better quality. Proteomics and metabolomics resources for agarwood analysis can clarify tree treatment mechanisms and support agarwood quality enhancement programs.
